title: systemd
subtitle: Every service in my estate that stays up is a locked-down systemd unit; the agent runtime, the credential service and the governance watcher among them.
lede: Auth and access plane holds the operations layer, and I wanted the fleet's behaviour fixed in configuration. A few dozen services sit under one stack target, with explicit ordering, and the unit files and an inventory are versioned with the code. PartOf cascades carry a dependency's restart through to its dependants, drop-ins make data-store clients wait for the network and declare cascade membership, and Docker-wrapped services are managed like native ones. Routine work such as container cleanup is a timer, visible and controllable on its own rather than a loop hidden in a script. The OAuth server faces the public, so its unit runs sandboxed.
quote: I build services to be operated: declared dependencies, sandboxing on anything public, secrets handled by the init system and recurring work in the open.
evidence: Linux service operations with systemd: a declared fleet under one stack target, with PartOf restart cascades and timers instead of hidden loops.
Sandboxing and container hardening: the public OAuth server's unit with no new privileges, a read-only system, a system-call filter and a memory limit, secrets through LoadCredential.
Inference serving architecture: pipeline services each restartable on its own, so one can be upgraded without draining the pipeline.
author: Corey James
